title: Windowed Throttle Coordinator and Queue-Freeze Protocol
creator: Asha Patel
description:
Background: Dedicated pools currently rely on static per-tenant rate caps and a best-effort queue. During transient spikes this leads to long tail latency for some tenants, unpredictable cache-priming costs, and noisy autoscaler behaviour. Goal: Implement a windowed throttle coordinator that enforces per-tenant burst budgets in sliding time windows and coordinates with the autoscaler to avoid instability. Complement the coordinator with a Queue-Freeze Protocol: when a tenant exceeds sustained budget thresholds, we freeze new queued requests for that tenant and surface a fast-fail or fallback path, while allowing a small slowpath window for critical low-latency requests.

Design summary: 1) Windowed budgets: track two sliding windows per tenant (short-burst: 10s, sustained: 5m) in a compact token-bucket-like register. Tokens are consumed by admitted requests; refills are time-decayed. Budgets are configurable per-plan (free/standard/premium) and influenced by guaranteed min-throughput commitments. 2) Coordinator service: a lightweight, sharded in-memory service co-located with fleet edge routing that enforces admission decisions (allow/queue/freeze/shed) and emits events. It supports local fast-path decisions using recent-window approximations and fallback to the coordinator state when uncertain. 3) Queue-Freeze Protocol: when sustained-window exhaustion is detected, the router transitions tenant queues into a frozen state for a short cooldown (configurable). Frozen queues reject new enqueues with an explicit error code and optional suggest-backoff header. Existing inflight requests are allowed to finish; a configurable reserve (e.g., 2 concurrent slots) remains for critical traffic annotated with a priority header. 4) Autoscaler coupling: coordinator exposes aggregate pressure signals (per-tenant and per-pool) to the autoscaler. Instead of immediate scale-ups at first spike, the autoscaler uses a hysteresis window and a prediction score to decide whether to scale or instruct the coordinator to increase preemptible burst capacity for a short interval.

API and config: - New route-level fields: tenant_window_params (short_window_sec, sustained_window_sec, short_limit, sustained_limit, reserve_slots) - Router headers: X-Tenant-Priority, X-Queue-Freeze-Reason - Error code for frozen enqueue: 429-FRZ with machine-readable retry-after and suggested-fallback fields

Trade-offs and alternatives considered: - Centralized vs fully local enforcement: we chose a hybrid sharded coordinator to keep global visibility for billing/guarantees but allow local fast decisions to minimize RTT. - Hard drop vs freeze: hard drops increase error rates and poor UX; freezing enables predictable behaviour and clearer signals to clients. - Complex ML prediction for autoscaling was deferred; we use simple trend+window heuristics for now to reduce implementation risk.

Metrics and telemetry: per-tenant short_window_util, sustained_window_util, freeze_events, freeze_duration, reserve_slot_usage, rejection_rate_with_reason, autoscaler_scale_suggestions, coordinator_decision_latency. Alerting: sustained_window_util > 90% for >5m (P1), freeze rate spike (P2).

Rollout plan: feature-flagged by pool. 1) Lab integration with synthetic tenant spike tests. 2) Canary in one US-dedicated pool with low-risk tenants, 48h monitoring. 3) Gradual ramp with automatic rollback on SLO regressions. 4) Multi-region rollout.

Acceptance criteria: - Coordinator makes admission decisions within 2ms median and 10ms p99 under normal load. - Freeze error code correctly returned and clients with reserve slots still admitted. - Autoscaler uses coordinator signals to reduce oscillatory scale-ups in synthetic tests by >50%. - No regression in global p50/p95 latency after canary compared to baseline.
